headline: If adopted, S. 2311 would have made it a federal crime to perform most abortions at 20 weeks or later, but the Senate did not take it up, so it did not become law.
what_it_does: The bill would have amended the federal criminal code to make it a crime to perform or attempt an abortion when the probable post-fertilization age of the fetus is 20 weeks or more. A violator would face a fine, up to five years in prison, or both. The bill would have allowed exceptions when the abortion is necessary to save the pregnant woman's life or when the pregnancy results from rape or incest, and a physician using an exception would have had to meet specified requirements. A woman who received a prohibited abortion would not have been prosecuted for violating or conspiring to violate the bill.

who_it_affects.group: Physicians and other providers who perform abortions
who_it_affects.how: They would have faced possible federal criminal fines and prison time for performing or attempting abortions at 20 weeks or later outside the listed exceptions, and would have had to meet extra requirements when using an exception.

who_it_affects.group: Pregnant women seeking abortions at 20 weeks or later
who_it_affects.how: They would not have been prosecuted under the bill for having a prohibited abortion or conspiring to have one.

who_it_affects.group: Hospitals and clinics that offer later-term abortions
who_it_affects.how: They would have needed to stop providing abortions at 20 weeks or later outside the bill's exceptions, since their staff could face federal criminal penalties.
